beef-noodles-and-vegetables-excluding-ca.title: Beef with noodles and vegetables without carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens; soy‑based sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of tender beef strips, boiled noodles and a mix of vegetables, excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens. It is seasoned with a soy‑based sauce that gives a rich umami flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is a high‑quality source of complete protein containing all essential amino acids.
Traditional wheat noodles cook quickly and absorb the sauce flavor well.
Omitting carrots and broccoli reduces beta‑carotene content while still providing vitamin C from peppers.
Soy sauce originated in China over 2,500 years ago and remains a staple in many world cuisines.
The dish can be adapted for dietary needs by swapping regular noodles for whole‑grain or gluten‑free versions.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed and supports normal blood formation.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: High‑quality protein aids muscle growth and recovery after exercise.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the noodles supply quick energy, useful for post‑workout replenishment.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and soy sauce are good sources of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of soy sauce
items.content: Fermented soy products contain polyphenols that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is salty; people with hypertension should limit their intake.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Beef can be high in saturated fat, so choosing lean cuts is advisable.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: The dish is calorie‑dense; overeating may contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, mixing beef, noodles and vegetables together and drizzling with soy sauce. Optional additions include fresh ginger, garlic or sliced green onions for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat with a splash of water or extra sauce to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoflower is a hybrid of broccoli and cauliflower created through selective breeding. When cooked it retains a bright green color, a mild flavor and a slightly crisp texture. It is commonly used in side dishes, salads and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoflower combines the nutritional profile of both broccoli and cauliflower.
It contains more vitamin C than regular broccoli.
Visually it looks like small cauliflower florets but has a softer bite.
In the United States it is often called “green cauliflower” or “broccoflower”.
Several cultivars exist, differing in floret shape and size.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked broccoflower provides about 30 kcal, making it ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Phytochemicals
items.content: Glucoraphanin and sulforaphane have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Cruciferous vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to broccoli, cauliflower and their hybrids.

items.title: High vitamin K content
items.content: Large amounts can interfere with blood‑thinning medication in susceptible people.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Raw florets may cause gas; cooking reduces this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Broccoflower can be boiled, steamed or lightly sautéed. Add it to salads, stews, pasta dishes, or serve as a side to meat and fish. A 5‑7 minute boil keeps the color vibrant and the texture crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. Freeze in freezer bags for longer storage (up to 8 months). Discard if you notice off‑odors, slime or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Candy is a sweet confection made from sugar, syrups, flavorings and various additives (fruits, nuts, gelatin, etc.). This type falls under the “non‑chocolate, other” category and is classified in the NFS system with code 5103.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest candy recipes were recorded in China more than 2,000 years ago.
In the Soviet era candies were often called “sweets” and used as holiday gifts.
There are over 1,000 varieties of candy: chewy, caramel, gummy, hard‑candy, and more.
Most modern candies are produced on automated lines where each ingredient is weighed to the gram.
In some countries candy is considered part of cultural heritage and featured in national food festivals.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Candy provides rapid glucose, which can be useful when blood‑sugar levels are low.

items.title: Mood boost
items.content: Sugar stimulates serotonin production, improving mood and giving a sense of pleasure.

items.title: Source of added vitamins
items.content: Candies fortified with vitamins (e.g., vitamin C or B‑complex) can contribute small amounts of these nutrients.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to weight gain, tooth decay, and metabolic disturbances.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Many candies contain nuts, dairy, gluten, and food colorings that may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Artificial additives
items.content: Some candies include artificial flavors and preservatives, which may have adverse health effects when eaten frequently.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Candies are typically enjoyed in small portions as a dessert or snack. They can be added to baked goods, ice cream, yogurt, or used as cake decorations.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store candies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent melting and texture changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Dressing with meat and vegetables is a ready‑to‑eat sauce that combines cooked or roasted meat, fresh or boiled vegetables, and aromatic spices. It is often used as a quick meal or as a complement to side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat‑and‑vegetable dressings are popular in Mediterranean and Eastern European cuisines.
The combination of protein and fiber makes them a satisfying lunch option.
Olive oil or other vegetable oils are frequently added, giving the dish a smooth flavor.
Preparation often involves braising meat with vegetables in their own juices, preserving most vitamins.
The dressing can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or frozen for longer shelf life.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables supply vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium, supporting immunity and heart function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Absence of added sugars makes the product suitable for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: When olive oil is used, the dressing contains monounsaturated fats that benefit vascular health.

items.title: Satiety and energy
items.content: The mix of protein, fat and fiber promotes prolonged fullness.

items.title: Allergy to meat or spices
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to certain meats or added spices.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared dressings often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage can lead to pathogen growth; adhere to recommended storage times and temperatures.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Recipes with generous amounts of oil can be calorie‑dense.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dressing can be served on its own, tossed into salads, used as a sandwich filling, or as a side for grains and potatoes. When reheating, do so over medium heat to preserve vegetable texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dressing in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Before consumption, heat thoroughly to at least 75 °C.

light-ice-cream-cone-vanilla-prepackaged.title: Light Ice Cream Cone, Vanilla, Prepackaged

content.title: About
content.content: Light vanilla ice cream cone is a ready‑to‑eat dessert packaged individually. It is made from low‑fat milk, cream, sugar and natural vanilla flavor, making it less caloric than traditional ice cream cones.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The thin wafer cone provides a crunchy texture and can be eaten without additional dishes.
Vanilla flavor is often derived from natural extracts, though synthetic substitutes are used for consistent taste.
Packaging is usually aluminum foil, protecting the product from light and moisture and extending shelf life.
Light versions often contain less fat by using skim milk and cream substitutes.
Portion‑size cones are popular in schools and offices because of their convenience and long shelf life.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using skim milk reduces saturated fat content, which can support a healthier diet.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Dairy ingredients provide calcium essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream supply vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Natural flavor
items.content: Vanilla extract contains antioxidants that may help protect cells.

items.title: Moderate sugar level
items.content: Compared with regular ice cream, light versions often have reduced sugar, aiding blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains dairy, so people with lactose intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein or whey proteins.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite reduction, it still contains sugar, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Storage at high temperatures
items.content: Prolonged storage above ‑4 °C can cause melting, affecting texture and flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The cone is ready to eat straight from the package. It can be enjoyed on its own, paired with fresh berries, or drizzled with a small amount of chocolate sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at ‑18 °C or lower. Once opened, consume within 24 hours to maintain optimal texture and taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Lactose‑free low‑fat milk (1 %) is pasteurized cow’s milk that has had the lactose removed and the fat content reduced. It retains the natural milky flavor while being suitable for people with lactose intolerance and those watching their fat intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lactose is removed using lactase enzyme treatment or ultrafiltration.
Low‑fat milk still provides about 30 % of the calcium found in whole milk.
Lactose‑free milk is popular in sports nutrition because of its low fat and high protein content.
In many markets it is labeled as “Lactose‑Free” or “No Lactose”.
Low‑fat variants generally have a longer shelf life after opening compared with whole milk.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Milk is one of the best dietary sources of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Even with reduced fat, the milk retains most of its casein and whey proteins, supporting muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: At 1 % fat, it fits well into calorie‑controlled and low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Suitable for lactose intolerance
items.content: The removal of lactose allows those with lactase deficiency to enjoy milk without digestive discomfort.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to casein or whey and must avoid all dairy products.

items.title: Added sugars
items.content: Although lactose is removed, some brands add sweeteners; always check the label.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Stabilizers or flavorings may be included to improve taste and texture, which could be an issue for sensitive consumers.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lactose‑free milk can have a slightly higher pH, which may cause mild stomach discomfort in very sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink it plain, add to cereals, smoothies, coffee, baking recipes, or sauces. It pairs well with fruit, berries, and whole grains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as it may affect texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat milk with 2 % milk fat is a pasteurised dairy product obtained from cow’s milk after part of the cream has been removed. It retains most of the nutrients of whole milk while providing fewer calories and less fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Reduced‑fat milk is a staple in many diet plans because of its lower fat content.
Mass production of reduced‑fat milk in the 20th century helped popularise low‑fat dairy products.
Milk with 2 % fat is considered a compromise between whole milk (3.5 %) and skim milk (0 %).
In some countries 2 % milk is called “light” or “low‑fat” milk.
Pasteurisation kills pathogenic bacteria while preserving most vitamins and minerals.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Milk is one of the best dietary sources of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption and supports the immune system.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Milk protein (casein and whey) aids muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The 2 % fat level reduces caloric intake while keeping a creamy taste.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B2 and B12 support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People lacking sufficient lactase may experience bloating, gas, and diarrhea after drinking milk.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions can range from skin rashes to anaphylaxis and require complete avoidance of dairy.

items.title: Hormone and antibiotic residues
items.content: In some regions milk may contain trace amounts of growth hormones or antibiotics, so choosing certified products is advisable.

items.title: Reduced fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Lower fat content means less vitamin A and E, which are naturally present in whole milk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reduced‑fat milk can be drunk plain, added to cereals, smoothies, coffee, baked goods, and sauces. It works well in protein shakes or as a substitute for whole milk when a recipe calls for a modest amount of fat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store milk in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not leave milk at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent bacterial growth.

potato-baked-peel-not-eaten-with-chili.title: Baked Potato, Peel Not Eaten, with Chili

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato without the skin, seasoned with hot chili, is a nutritious dish popular in many world cuisines. The potato retains most of its vitamins and minerals, while chili adds a spicy aroma and can boost metabolism.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is the fourth most produced agricultural crop worldwide after rice, wheat, and corn.
Baking breaks down starch, making it more digestible than raw potato.
Chili contains capsaicin, which may increase metabolic rate and has mild analgesic effects.
In several cultures, baked potatoes with chili are sold as street food, for example in Mexico and the United States.
Potato skin is rich in fiber, but this recipe removes it to lower phytate content.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Potatoes provide vitamin C, supporting the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Both chili and potato contain antioxidants such as carotenoids and polyphenols that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Partially gelatinized starch from baking is easier to digest, and a modest amount of fiber aids bowel regularity.

items.title: Metabolism boost
items.content: Capsaicin in chili can increase thermogenesis, helping the body burn more calories.

items.title: Spicy heat
items.content: Large amounts of chili may cause stomach irritation or heartburn, especially in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience allergic reactions to potato, manifesting as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the dish is seasoned with salt, monitor intake to avoid excessive sodium.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Baked potato has a high glycemic index, which can raise blood sugar quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hot baked potato without skin, sprinkled with chili and, if desired, a drizzle of olive oil or a dollop of sour cream. It can be added to salads, used as a side for meat or fish, or enjoyed as a standalone snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave to restore a crisp texture.

rice-brown-with-peas-and-carrots-fat-add.title: Brown Rice with Peas and Carrots, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice mixed with peas and carrots and enriched with plant fat is a whole‑grain product that combines the nutritional benefits of brown rice, the protein of peas, the vitamins of carrots, and the energy‑dense fat, making it a balanced meal for active lifestyles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, providing more fiber and B‑vitamins than white rice.
Peas are a good source of plant protein, vitamin C, and folate.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A for vision and immunity.
Adding plant fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) from carrots.
The dish is popular in sports nutrition because it offers a mix of carbs, protein, and fats.

items.title: Sustained Energy
items.content: Complex carbohydrates in brown rice provide a steady release of glucose, supporting endurance during workouts and mental tasks.

items.title: Protein Boost
items.content: Peas contribute about 5 g of protein per 100 g of the product, aiding muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and Minerals
items.content: Carrots supply beta‑carotene, while brown rice offers magnesium, phosphorus, and iron, essential for bone health and blood formation.

items.title: Digestive Support
items.content: Fiber from whole‑grain rice and peas promotes healthy bowel movements and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Improved Nutrient Absorption
items.content: The added fat helps the body better absorb the fat‑soluble vitamins present in carrots.

items.title: Pea Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rash to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: High Caloric Content
items.content: The added fat increases the calorie density, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Phytate Content
items.content: Brown rice contains phytates, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Oxalate Levels
items.content: Carrots contain modest amounts of oxalates; people prone to kidney stones should consume the product in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish can be served as a side, a main meal, or added to salads, wraps, and bowls. It reheats well in the microwave, and a sprinkle of fresh herbs adds extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life store it in the refrigerator, where it remains good for up to 6 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork tamale is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of corn masa filled with seasoned pork, chilies, garlic and spices, wrapped in a corn husk and steamed until tender.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales are among the oldest foods in the Americas, dating back to the Maya and Aztec civilizations.
The masa is made from nixtamalized corn flour, which gives it a distinctive aroma and yellowish hue.
Regional variations may include chicken, beef, cheese, vegetables, or even sweet fillings.
Tamales are commonly served at celebrations such as Day of the Dead and Christmas.
The corn husk wrapper imparts a subtle flavor and keeps the tamale moist during cooking.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The pork filling provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Pork supplies vitamin B12, important for nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from the meat helps maintain hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates from masa
items.content: Corn masa releases energy slowly, promoting lasting satiety.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: The corn husk and part of the masa add fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tamales are often seasoned with salt and sauces, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Pork contains saturated fats; moderate consumption is advised for those monitoring cholesterol.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked tamales can harbor salmonella or other bacteria.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to corn products, including the masa.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tamales are served hot, unwrapped from the corn husk. They can be enjoyed plain or topped with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or a spicy chili sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked tamales in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑lock bag for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.
